title: One-shot game using Opus 5.5. This model is insane!
author: mnm9678
selftext:
Made this today using new Opus 5.5.  
  
My prompt was "build me a AAA 3d game about a dimension hopping cyberpunk drifter, include menu, music and make sure graphics are AAA quality with good story and level and environment design. Do 2 levels for now, each level is semi open world, each a different dimension with unique buildings, environments and npcs/characters and activities to make it feel open world (exploration, side quests, etc.). Make it feel like a real well produced AAA game with high visual fidelity. It should also support controller. Review and test periodically to ensure AAA quality".

All built with Three.js. All assets, environments, characters, sound effects and music procedurally generated. No tools.

Try it at [https://jaxum.vercel.app](https://jaxum.vercel.app/)

replies.author: mnm9678
replies.body:
If you mean an actual AAA production, nothing. That was the prompt, not the result.

What it did get is the AAA checklist stuff you rarely see in one-prompt demos like title menu, settings, save/continue, controller support, 2 semi-open levels with quests and collectibles, cinematic cameras etc.

The art is procedural geometry and shaders, and the NPCs look like mannequins up close. Imagine the same prompt but with access to things like Unreal engine, blender and an asset library.

replies.author: mnm9678
replies.body:
Fair question, so here's exactly what happened. I put one prompt, the one in the post, claude code then worked on its own for about 3.5 hours: it wrote a story doc first, split the work across sub-agents, and kept testing its own build, taking screenshots and running scripted playthroughs of the quests.

After that I sent two more messages: "deploy to vercel", and a bug report once I'd played it (the camera didn't follow the player after refreshing the page & continuing into level 2, and there was a black flicker). It fixed both. So one prompt for the game, one follow-up for bugs.

comments.author: CubersumGame
comments.body:
As before, I see no reason to equate these 'oneshots' with real games.

Typically, such oneshots only look cool. When you actually try to play them, you are bound to run into issues, glitches, and flaws. And that’s saying nothing of the fact that if you leave the plot and story decisions up to Opus, you'll likely end up with a severe glitch and a total loss of narrative at some point. As of right now, even the newest models can’t maintain story context properly (by the way, Opus is much worse at this than GPT or even Gemini).

You could say these are just minor details - but these details are exactly what constitutes the 'last mile.' After creating a oneshot in a few hours without any oversight, you will then spend months hunting down bugs.

This happens for a simple reason: if you know what is supposed to happen in the game, you can control the process. But if you don't know what's going to happen, you don't know at what exact point the whole thing will break down.

This is the main issue with oneshots, and it’s the reason why all those enthusiastic videos shouldn’t be taken seriously.

replies.author: robhanz
replies.body: These are interesting ways of getting a base structure in place to start the real work.

replies.author: mnm9678
replies.body:
Mostly agree, and this build proves your point a bit. When I played the deployed version I hit two bugs within minutes. The last mile is real.

Two things surprised me though:

1) It wrote its own tests before I touched it: scripted playthroughs of both levels' main quests and level 1's side quests, tests that try to escape the map, parkour jump checks, and a gamepad simulation. 

Those caught real bugs during the build. My two slipped through because nothing tested "refresh, then Continue into level 2" or real frame pacing. After my report it reproduced both, added regression tests, and fixed them.

2) On story: it wrote a story bible first and generated all dialogue trees and the quests from it, so it stays consistent across two levels. Whether that holds for a 20-hour game, no idea.

So not shippable, but further along than "looks cool, falls apart on contact."

comments.author: YYY003003
comments.body:
Nice thanks for showing me this. I disagree with everyone here though, these one shot prompts are always a good baseline to get an idea of the intelligence of a model because it shows how long an LLM can go before falling into mediocrity, and with each new model we can see it go a little further.

  
A few years ago a state of the art LLM would make a bunch of stick figures on a flat green floor and tell you with a straight face the game is done and then it would crash on startup.
